sections.question: Which information is used to link a Compass Card when activating U-Pass BC?
sections.explanation: SFU says to link the Compass Card by entering the 20-digit number and CVN from the back of the card.

children.text: Your SFU Computing ID is used to sign in, while the number and CVN on your Compass Card are used to link the card.
Hypothetical example:
Sam signs in through the U-Pass BC website, selects Simon Fraser University, links a Compass Card using its number and CVN, and then requests the U-Pass BC.

items.question: Is my SFU Computing ID the same login used for SFU email?

children.text: Yes. SFU identifies it as the same login used for SFU email.

items.question: Where are the Compass Card details needed for linking?

children.text: The 20-digit number and CVN are on the back of the Compass Card.

sections.question: Which option can a student use if a semester permit is sold out?

options.text: Join the waitlist and use daily parking or a FlexPass
Park for free anywhere on Burnaby campus

sections.explanation: SFU says students may join the waitlist and choose daily parking, a FlexPass, or another available permit. Burnaby campus does not offer free parking, and students cannot buy monthly permits.

children.text: Consider how often you expect to drive. SFU identifies daily parking for occasional visits, FlexPass for some recurring visits, and semester permits for students who drive frequently. Permit availability may be limited.
Hypothetical example:
A student expects to drive only occasionally. Instead of seeking a semester permit, they choose daily parking and pay through an accepted method.

items.question: Is free parking available at SFU Burnaby?

children.text: No. SFU states that all Burnaby campus parking is paid through a permit, pay station, or app.

items.question: What happens if a semester permit is sold out?

children.text: Join the waitlist. While waiting, you can select another available permit or purchase daily parking or a FlexPass.

sections.question: Where must an SFU Surrey permit holder park in the Central City Mall parkade?
sections.explanation: The P3 level is reserved for SFU permit holders. The SFU parking FAQ says permit holders may receive a ticket if they park on another level.

children.text: A student must be registered for classes at the Surrey campus to qualify for a Surrey parking permit. Permit holders use the designated P3 level at Central City Mall.
Hypothetical example:
Sam has a Surrey parking permit. Before class, Sam enters the Central City Mall parkade and parks on P3 rather than another level.

items.question: Who qualifies for a student parking permit at Surrey campus?

children.text: A student must be registered for classes at the Surrey campus.

items.question: Where can someone without an SFU permit find parking information?

children.text: The SFU parking FAQ directs non-permit holders to information about alternate paid parking locations.

sections.question: Which statement about parking at SFU's Vancouver campus is correct?

options.text: SFU has designated parking facilities there.
Drivers can use public parking garages in the area.
Only street parking is available nearby.

sections.explanation: SFU does not have designated parking facilities at its Vancouver campus. Public parking garages are available nearby.

children.text: When driving to SFU Vancouver, plan to use a public garage rather than an SFU parking facility.
Hypothetical example:
Before visiting Harbour Centre, Sam checks the location of a nearby public garage and chooses one that suits the visit.

items.question: Does SFU provide designated parking at its Vancouver campus?

children.text: No. The source says there are no designated SFU parking facilities at the Vancouver campus.

items.question: Are public garages available near SFU Vancouver?

children.text: Yes. Public parking garages are available in the area, including garages near Harbour Centre and other SFU Vancouver buildings.

sections.question: According to SFU, who may find a FlexPass multipack suitable?

options.text: Someone driving to campus about 1 or 2 days a week
Someone looking for free parking at Burnaby campus
Someone parking in a restricted lot

sections.explanation: SFU says a FlexPass may suit someone who drives to campus about 1 or 2 days a week. Burnaby campus has no free parking, and FlexPass is not valid in restricted lots.

children.text: FlexPass is one option for occasional campus driving. SFU describes it as a discounted multipack of daily permits that can be used in multiple lots.
Hypothetical example:
A student drives to campus once a week. They compare FlexPass with daily parking and confirm that their planned lot accepts FlexPass before parking.

items.question: Is parking free at SFU's Burnaby campus?

children.text: No. SFU says all Burnaby campus parking is paid through a permit, pay station, or app.

items.question: What can a driver do if a parking permit is sold out?

children.text: SFU says they can join the waitlist and consider an alternate permit, daily parking, or FlexPass.

sections.question: Which response best shows clear and respectful workplace communication?

options.text: State your concern calmly and ask a follow-up question.
Use complicated terms to sound more professional.
Interrupt so your opinion is heard first.

sections.explanation: Calmly sharing a concern and asking a question supports clarity, listening, and respectful discussion.

children.text: Simple language and follow-up questions can reduce misunderstandings. After a discussion, a written summary can confirm important points.
Hypothetical example:
A worker is unsure who will complete part of a project. They calmly ask, “Could we confirm who is responsible for this task?” After the meeting, they send a short email summarizing the answer.

items.question: What can I do if a workplace expectation is unclear?

children.text: Observe how the workplace operates and ask a supervisor or coworker a clear question.

items.question: How can I show that I am listening?

children.text: Pay attention and ask a relevant follow-up question.

sections.question: Who needs a SIN for employment purposes?

options.text: Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and temporary residents who work in Canada

sections.explanation: A SIN is needed for employment purposes by Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and temporary residents who are authorized to work.

children.text: A SIN is used to manage employment records, tax filings, and access to government programs. It is confidential and is not a form of identification.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is authorized to work in Canada and accepts a job. Sam applies for a SIN and provides the number to the employer for income reporting.

items.question: Do students need a SIN to apply to a post-secondary school?

children.text: No. A SIN is not needed to apply to a university, college, or other post-secondary institution. It may be needed later for tax or education-benefit purposes.

items.question: Is a SIN a form of identification?

children.text: No. It is a confidential number used for administrative purposes.

sources.title: The Social Insurance Number (SIN) Code of Practice
SIN for temporary residents in Canada

sections.question: Which document confirms identity when a temporary resident applies for a SIN?

options.text: A passport or government-issued driver's licence

sections.explanation: A temporary resident must provide a secondary identity document, such as a passport or government-issued driver's licence. An IRCC email is not accepted as the document authorizing work.

children.text: Temporary residents need a valid work permit, study permit, or visitor record that authorizes work. They also need a secondary document confirming their identity.
Hypothetical example:
Sam checks that their valid work permit and passport are ready, then chooses to apply online.

items.question: Is a SIN confirmation letter an identity document?

children.text: No. It has no photo or security features and is not a piece of identification.

items.question: What if the name on my documents does not match my current name?

children.text: You need to provide a supporting document when applying.

sources.title: SIN for temporary residents in Canada

sections.question: Which document can confirm a temporary resident's identity for a SIN application?
sections.explanation: A passport is an accepted example of a secondary identity document. IRCC email messages are not accepted, and a SIN confirmation letter is not identification.

children.text: Temporary residents must provide a valid IRCC document that authorizes them to work, plus a secondary document that confirms their identity.
Hypothetical example:
Sam checks that their valid work permit and passport are ready before starting the SIN application.

items.question: Can a temporary resident use an IRCC email instead of a valid permit?

children.text: No. IRCC email messages are not accepted as the document authorizing work.

items.question: What if the name on the documents does not match?

children.text: A supporting document is needed when the current name differs from the name on the other documents.

sources.title: SIN for temporary residents in Canada

sections.question: Which request is an appropriate reason to provide your SIN?

options.text: Your employer requests it after you begin working
A landlord requests it as identification
A casual acquaintance asks to record it

sections.explanation: Employers must collect an employee's SIN for income tax and benefit purposes. A SIN is confidential and is not an identity document.

children.text: When an organization requests your SIN, ask why it needs the number and whether the law requires you to provide it. A private organization cannot require a SIN for a purpose other than income reporting.
Hypothetical example:
A rental company asks Sam for a SIN to confirm identity. Sam asks why it is needed and declines because a SIN is not an identity document.

items.question: Is a SIN a form of identification?

children.text: No. It is a confidential number used for administrative purposes.

items.question: Must I provide my SIN for a credit check?

children.text: No. You are not legally required to provide it for a credit check. A credit report without your SIN may be offered instead.

sources.title: The Social Insurance Number (SIN) Code of Practice

sections.question: Which situation requires a SIN?

options.text: Using a SIN as photo identification

sections.explanation: A SIN is needed for employment. It is not required to apply for post-secondary education and is not an identity document.

children.text: A SIN is confidential administrative information. An employer uses it to report employment income for tax and benefit purposes.
Hypothetical example:
Priya begins a new job and gives her SIN directly to her employer for income reporting. She does not use her SIN confirmation letter as identification.

items.question: Is a SIN a form of identification?

children.text: No. A SIN is a confidential number used for administrative purposes.

items.question: Do all bank accounts require a SIN?

children.text: No. Certain financial institutions must request it for accounts and investments that pay income, such as interest or dividends.

sources.title: The Social Insurance Number (SIN) Code of Practice

sections.question: What is true about a Social Insurance Number?

options.text: It is a confidential number for administrative purposes.
It is a photo identity document.
It can be shared whenever someone asks for it.

sections.explanation: A SIN is confidential and is not an identity document. Provide it only when the law requires it or when you understand why it is needed and accept the risks.

children.text: A SIN is personal information. Before sharing it, ask why it is needed and whether the law requires it.
Hypothetical example:
A store asks Sam for a SIN during a purchase. Sam asks why it is needed before deciding whether to provide it.

items.question: Is a SIN an identity document?

children.text: No. A SIN is a confidential number used for administrative purposes.

items.question: When should a temporary resident update their SIN record?

children.text: They should update it after receiving a new permit with a new expiry date, or when their immigration status or legal name changes.

sources.title: The Social Insurance Number (SIN) Code of Practice
SIN for temporary residents in Canada

sections.question: Where can a student ask for guidance about getting involved in the campus community?
sections.explanation: A Student Life team member at the Hub can guide students who are unsure how to get involved.

children.text: Student Life offers different ways to participate, including clubs, volunteering, and campus recreation. A student can choose an option that fits their interests.
Hypothetical example:
Sam wants to meet people who share an interest. Sam visits the Hub and asks a Student Life team member about suitable clubs.

items.question: Are back-to-school events only for new students?

children.text: No. Langara describes them as events for new and returning students.

items.question: Who can help if I am unsure how to get involved?

children.text: Visit the Hub and speak with a Student Life team member.

sources.title: Langara students share how they built their circle from day one

sections.question: Which Langara resource can guide a student who wants to get involved in campus life?

options.text: A Student Life team member at the Hub

sections.explanation: Langara says students can visit the Hub and speak with a Student Life team member for guidance on getting involved.

children.text: LSU services are one part of campus life. Langara also offers clubs, volunteering, recreation, events, and drop-in opportunities that can help students connect with others and develop skills.
Hypothetical example:
A student visits the LSU building to learn about its services. They also ask a Student Life team member at the Hub about clubs and volunteering that match their interests.

items.question: Where can I ask for help finding ways to get involved?

children.text: Visit the Hub in A140 and speak with a Student Life team member.

items.question: What are some ways to participate beyond LSU leadership?

children.text: Langara highlights student clubs, the VOLT Volunteer Program, campus recreation, events, and drop-in opportunities.

sources.title: Langara students share how they built their circle from day one

sections.question: Which Langara service can provide health information and connect students with helpful resources?

options.text: Registered nurses from the Student Services Medical Clinic

sections.explanation: Registered nurses from the Student Services Medical Clinic can answer health questions, provide information, and connect students with helpful resources.

children.text: Knowing what kind of help you need can make it easier to choose a service. The Student Services Medical Clinic provides health information, while Counselling Services supports personal, educational, and career challenges.
Hypothetical example:
A student has a health question but does not know which resource to use. They contact the Student Services Medical Clinic to ask for information and help finding an appropriate resource.

items.question: Where can I ask a health question?

children.text: Registered nurses from the Student Services Medical Clinic can provide health information and connect you with helpful resources.

items.question: What kinds of challenges can Counselling Services help with?

children.text: Counselling Services supports personal, educational, and career challenges through sessions, groups, and workshops.

sections.question: Where can a student ask for guidance about getting involved in campus life?

options.text: The Student Life team at the Hub
A classroom during a scheduled lecture

sections.explanation: Langara directs students to speak with a Student Life team member at the Hub for guidance about getting involved.

children.text: Student Life offers several ways to participate, including clubs, volunteering, and campus recreation. A student can choose an option that fits their interests.
Hypothetical example:
A student is unsure which activity suits them. They visit the Hub and ask a Student Life team member about ways to participate.

items.question: What if I am not sure how I want to get involved?

children.text: Speak with a Student Life team member at the Hub for guidance.

items.question: Are campus activities only for new students?

children.text: No. Langara’s Back to School events are designed for new and returning students.

sources.title: Langara students share how they built their circle from day one

sections.question: Where can a student ask for guidance about getting involved on campus?

options.text: The Student Life team at the Hub
A classroom during a scheduled course

sections.explanation: Langara directs students to the Student Life team at the Hub for guidance about getting involved.

children.text: Student Life offers several ways to connect, including clubs, volunteering, and campus recreation. A student can ask the Student Life team for help choosing a suitable path.
Hypothetical example:
A student wants to meet people but is unsure which activity fits. They visit the Hub and ask a Student Life team member about available ways to participate.

items.question: What if I am unsure how I want to get involved?

children.text: Speak with a Student Life team member at the Hub for guidance.

items.question: Are clubs the only way to participate in campus life?

children.text: No. Langara also identifies volunteering and campus recreation as ways to participate.

sources.title: Langara students share how they built their circle from day one

sections.question: Which Langara program offers volunteering as a way to build skills and confidence?
sections.explanation: VOLT is Langara's volunteering program. It supports giving back, connecting with others, and developing skills and confidence.

children.text: Volunteer experience can demonstrate hard and soft skills. When describing it, identify what you did and the skills you developed.
Hypothetical example:
A student helps at a VOLT event and works with other volunteers. Later, the student describes the experience as evidence of teamwork and growing confidence.

items.question: Where can I ask for help finding a way to get involved?

children.text: Speak with a Student Life team member at the Hub in A140 or email volt@langara.ca.

items.question: What are some other ways to participate in campus life?

children.text: Students can explore clubs, Campus Recreation, Langara Falcons, back-to-school events, and drop-in opportunities.

sources.title: Langara students share how they built their circle from day one

sections.question: Which goal is measurable and time-bound?

options.text: Complete a spreadsheet course by the end of the month.

sections.explanation: The correct goal names an observable result and gives a clear time frame.

children.text: An objective describes an action needed to reach a goal. If one objective becomes crowded with several outcomes, separate it into smaller objectives so each remains specific.
Hypothetical example:
A job seeker wants to strengthen interview skills. One objective could be: “By the end of the workshop, I will be able to demonstrate how to answer a practice interview question.”

items.question: What can make progress measurable?

children.text: Use an indicator that shows whether the intended action or outcome happened.

items.question: Can a goal have more than one objective?

children.text: Yes. Several focused objectives may be clearer than trying to fit everything into one.

lessons.title: Lesson 8.1: What you'll see in your account

sections.question: What does “Waiting on you” mean in the application status tracker?

options.text: IRCC needs more information or documents from you
IRCC has finished reviewing the entire application
IRCC has not received the application

sections.explanation: “Waiting on you” means IRCC needs information or documents from you. Check the “Your next steps” section for details.

children.text: A status applies to a particular part of an application. “Completed” means IRCC finished reviewing that section, not necessarily the entire application.
Hypothetical example:
Sam sees that biometrics are “Completed,” while background verification is “In progress.” This means the biometrics section is finished, but the background section is still being reviewed.

items.question: When do status updates appear in the tracker?

children.text: They appear after you receive an acknowledgment of receipt letter or email.

items.question: Where can I see whether IRCC needs something from me?

children.text: Check the “Your next steps” section regularly for requests for information, documents, or other actions.

sources.title: What does my status mean in the application status tracker?

sections.question: What does a sponsor promise by signing an undertaking?

options.text: To provide financial support for the sponsored family member's basic needs
To guarantee that the application will be approved
To exempt the family member from medical checks

sections.explanation: An undertaking is a binding promise to provide financial support for basic needs. It does not guarantee approval or remove application checks.

children.text: The sponsorship undertaking remains a binding promise of support for its applicable period, even if the sponsor’s circumstances or relationship change.
Hypothetical example:

After sponsoring a spouse, Alex organizes copies of the signed undertaking and supporting records in one folder. Alex understands that a later separation would not automatically cancel the undertaking.

items.question: Must family members be declared in a permanent residence application?

children.text: Yes. The guide says all family members must be declared and examined, even if they will not come to Canada with the principal applicant.

items.question: Can a permanent resident living outside Canada sponsor from abroad?

children.text: No. The guide says permanent residents living abroad cannot sponsor from outside Canada.

sources.title: Sponsor your spouse, common-law partner, conjugal partner or dependent child – Complete Guide (IMM 5289)

sections.question: What is a clear way to contribute to a workplace decision?

options.text: Share a relevant suggestion with the team

sections.explanation: Clear communication includes openly sharing relevant ideas and opinions. Listening and asking follow-up questions also support collaboration.

children.text: Workplace beliefs can shape decisions. A workplace that values teamwork may invite people to collaborate, while one that values innovation may support new ideas. Observe local practices and ask questions when expectations are unclear.
Hypothetical example:
During a meeting, Sam notices that task updates are unclear. Sam respectfully suggests brief check-ins, listens to the team’s responses, and summarizes the agreed plan in a follow-up email.

items.question: How can I learn how decisions are made in my workplace?

children.text: Observe workplace practices and ask questions when expectations are unclear.

items.question: How can I disagree or suggest a change clearly?

children.text: Share your idea in simple language, listen actively, and ask follow-up questions.

sections.question: What should you determine before choosing an investment?

options.text: Your risk tolerance and when you will need the money
Only the name of the financial institution

sections.explanation: Your comfort with risk and the time available for your goal help you assess whether an investment may be suitable.

children.text: The time available for a goal affects how you save and invest. A longer timeline may allow consideration of a broader range of investments, but every investment still involves risk.
Hypothetical example:

Sam is saving for retirement. Before selecting investments, Sam writes down the goal, considers when the money will be needed, reviews personal comfort with possible losses, and checks the investments and fees.

items.question: What does compound interest mean?

children.text: It is interest earned on the original deposit and on interest earned in earlier periods.

items.question: What should I check when considering a mutual fund?

children.text: Understand its mix of investments, objectives, and fees because these can affect your return.

sections.question: Which action best shows respectful workplace communication?

options.text: Listen carefully and ask a follow-up question
Ignore a coworker who is speaking
Use complicated terms when simple words are clear

sections.explanation: Listening carefully and asking relevant questions can show respect and help prevent misunderstandings.

children.text: Respectful communication includes listening actively, using clear language, and asking questions when expectations are unclear.
Hypothetical example:
A coworker explains a task. You listen, then politely ask a question to confirm what needs to be done.

items.question: How can I show respect when someone is speaking?

children.text: Pay attention and ask a relevant follow-up question if you need clarification.

items.question: What can I do if I am unsure about workplace expectations?

children.text: Observe how the workplace operates and ask questions about anything that is unclear.

sections.question: Which question best shows that you researched the role and want useful details?

options.text: What challenges do you expect the person in this role to face?

sections.explanation: A question about expected challenges helps you evaluate the role and shows informed interest. Basic information should be researched before the interview.

children.text: Research the company and job before the interview. Use that research to prepare questions that help you understand whether the opportunity fits your goals.
Hypothetical example:
Sam reads that a role involves project work. During the interview, Sam asks, “How does the team collaborate on projects?” The answer helps Sam understand how the team works.

items.question: What can I do if I do not understand an interview question?

children.text: Ask the interviewer for clarification rather than answering a question you may have misunderstood.

items.question: Can I ask about the interview format before the meeting?

children.text: Yes. When scheduling, you can ask whether there will be a test and how many people will attend.

sources.title: Preparing for an interview - Job Bank

sections.question: What should you compare before choosing a banking service?

options.text: How you will use it, its benefits, and any fees or rates
Only the name of the financial institution
Only the design of its mobile app

sections.explanation: A suitable service should meet your needs. Compare how you will use it, its benefits, and any applicable fees and rates.

children.text: Compare banking products by reviewing their features, fees, rates, and terms and conditions. A convenient service may still be unsuitable if its costs or features do not match your needs.
Hypothetical example:
Sam regularly pays bills and makes electronic transfers. Sam compares accounts based on those services and their fees, then chooses the account that best fits these day-to-day needs.

items.question: Which account is usually suited to day-to-day transactions?

children.text: A chequing account is usually suited to regular purchases, bill payments, withdrawals, and transfers.

items.question: What extra cost can overdraft protection involve?

children.text: It may involve interest and pay-per-use fees, so review the terms before using it.

sources.title: Choosing financial products and services that are right for you

sections.question: What does payment frequency describe?

options.text: How often mortgage payments are made
How long the mortgage contract is in effect
How long it takes to repay the mortgage fully

sections.explanation: Payment frequency is how often you make payments. The other options describe the term and amortization period.

children.text: A lender may offer monthly, semi-monthly, biweekly, weekly, or accelerated payment schedules. An accelerated schedule makes the equivalent of one extra monthly payment each year.
Hypothetical example:
Sam compares a standard biweekly schedule with an accelerated biweekly schedule. Sam asks the lender to explain how each option would affect the payment amount and interest costs.

items.question: What can a mortgage payment include?

children.text: It goes toward principal and interest. It may also include optional mortgage insurance or property taxes paid through the lender.

items.question: How does a longer amortization period affect costs?

children.text: Payments are typically lower because they are spread over more time, but more interest is paid overall.

sources.title: Choosing a mortgage that is right for you

sections.question: What may happen when interest rates rise on a variable-rate mortgage with fixed payments?

options.text: More of each payment may go toward interest
The interest rate becomes fixed automatically
The mortgage balance is paid off automatically

sections.explanation: When rates rise, more of a fixed payment may go toward interest, leaving less to reduce the principal.

children.text: A variable-rate mortgage may have fixed or adjustable payments. With fixed payments, a rate increase sends more of each payment toward interest. With adjustable payments, the payment amount changes when the rate changes.
Hypothetical example:

Sam compares two variable-rate mortgages. One keeps the payment fixed, while the other adjusts the payment when the rate changes. Sam asks the lender how each option would affect the principal if rates rise.

items.question: Can a variable-rate mortgage keep the same payment amount?

children.text: Yes. Some have fixed payments even though the interest rate changes.

items.question: Can different parts of a hybrid mortgage have different terms?

children.text: Yes. This may make the mortgage harder to transfer to another lender.

sources.title: Choosing a mortgage that is right for you

sections.question: Which schedule makes the equivalent of one extra monthly payment each year?
sections.explanation: Accelerated biweekly payments equal one extra monthly payment each year, which can reduce the principal faster and lower interest costs.

children.text: Mortgage contracts differ in flexibility. An open mortgage generally permits more extra payments, while a closed mortgage usually limits them. A contract’s prepayment privileges explain what extra payments are allowed.
Hypothetical example:
Sam expects occasional extra income. Before choosing a mortgage, Sam compares each contract’s prepayment privileges and asks the lender about limits and possible penalties.

items.question: What does payment frequency mean?

children.text: It means how often you make mortgage payments. Available schedules may include monthly, semi-monthly, biweekly, weekly, and accelerated options.

items.question: What should I check if I may sell my home during the mortgage term?

children.text: Ask about penalties for breaking the contract and whether the mortgage is portable. A portable mortgage may let you transfer its balance, rate, and conditions, subject to lender eligibility and restrictions.

sources.title: Choosing a mortgage that is right for you

sections.question: Which SWOT pair describes external factors?
sections.explanation: Opportunities and threats come from outside the person. Strengths and weaknesses are internal.

children.text: A SWOT analysis can guide an action plan. Choose an action that builds on a positive factor or reduces a negative factor.
Hypothetical example:
Lee identifies specialized knowledge as a strength and a leadership opportunity as an external chance. Lee sets a goal to pursue that opportunity and apply the knowledge.

items.question: Is a professional contact a strength or an opportunity?

children.text: An existing network of contacts can be an internal strength. A new networking event can be an external opportunity.

items.question: What should I do after completing a SWOT analysis?

children.text: Use the findings to choose goals and specific next actions.

sections.question: Which finding on your credit report may be a sign of identity theft?

options.text: An account you did not open
A payment correctly marked as on time

sections.explanation: An unfamiliar account may mean someone applied for credit in your name.

children.text: A credit report can contain personal details, account information, balances, and payment history. Reviewing reports from both main credit bureaus can help you notice errors or possible fraud sooner.
Hypothetical example:
Alex reviews both credit reports and finds an account they did not open. Alex contacts the affected lender and both credit bureaus about the suspected fraud.

items.question: Does checking your own credit report or score lower your credit score?

children.text: No. Checking your own report or score does not affect your credit score.

items.question: What documents can help when disputing an error?

children.text: Collect receipts, statements, and other documents that show the information is wrong.

sources.title: Checking your credit report for errors and fraud

sections.question: What is an appropriate way to learn from a job rejection?

options.text: Demand that the employer change the decision
Assume the rejection proves you are unqualified

sections.explanation: Feedback may identify an area to improve. A rejection does not necessarily mean you are unqualified.

children.text: Consider several possible reasons for the decision instead of assuming you failed. The employer may have chosen an internal candidate or someone who better fit the team.
Hypothetical example:
Sam receives a rejection email. Sam replies politely, asks whether the interviewer can suggest an area to improve, and uses any feedback to prepare for another interview.

items.question: Does rejection mean I was not qualified?

children.text: Not necessarily. The employer may have selected another candidate for reasons such as team fit or an internal application.

items.question: What if the employer does not provide feedback?

children.text: Reflect on what went well and what you would adjust in your next interview.

sources.title: Seven tips on how to deal with job rejection

sections.question: What is the most respectful action before entering a room?

options.text: Stand very close to the doorway

sections.explanation: Knocking gives people notice and respects their privacy.

children.text: Clear communication can help people understand one another’s comfort and expectations.
Hypothetical example:
A coworker steps back during a conversation. You allow more space and continue speaking politely.

items.question: Does stepping back during a conversation always mean someone is unfriendly?

children.text: No. They may simply be making themselves more comfortable.

items.question: What can I do if I am unsure about expectations in a workplace?

children.text: Observe the workplace and ask a clear question about its expectations.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.4: What To Do If You’re Targeted

sections.question: What should you do first if you suspect a scam?

options.text: Stop contact with the suspected scammer
Send more information to confirm the request
Forward the message to other people

sections.explanation: Stopping contact helps prevent the suspected scammer from getting more money or information.

children.text: After ending contact, secure any affected account and report the issue to the relevant provider. If a profile was hacked, changing its password can help protect it.
Hypothetical example:
Sam notices an unfamiliar message sent from their social media profile. Sam changes the password, uses the platform’s reporting features, and contacts the people who run the site.

items.question: What can I do if someone hacked my social media profile?

children.text: Change your password and use the account’s privacy and reporting features.

items.question: Should I keep suspicious online messages?

children.text: Keep relevant messages or screenshots as a record in case you need to show what happened.

sources.title: What to do if you're being cyberbullied

sections.question: What should you review to confirm which supporting documents your application needs?

options.text: The guide and checklist for your specific program
A document list from any immigration program
Only the list used by another applicant

sections.explanation: Each program has its own supporting-document requirements. Check the guide and checklist for your specific program.

children.text: Common supporting documents can include identity records, medical exams, police certificates, language tests, ECAs, and proof of funds. The exact requirements depend on the program.
Hypothetical example:
Sam reviews the guide and checklist for their chosen program, then organizes only the documents requested there.

items.question: Does every permanent residence application require the same documents?

children.text: No. Each program has its own supporting-document list.

items.question: What does an educational credential assessment show?

children.text: It shows that a degree, diploma, or certificate is valid and equal to a Canadian credential.

sections.question: Which action best shows interest during small talk?

options.text: Listen and ask a follow-up question
Change the topic before the person answers

sections.explanation: Listening and asking a follow-up question shows interest and supports clear, friendly communication.

children.text: A follow-up question can keep a friendly conversation going. Listen to the answer, then ask a simple question connected to what the person said.
Hypothetical example:
A coworker mentions weekend plans. You listen and ask, “What are you looking forward to?”

items.question: How can I show that I am listening?

children.text: Pay attention, nod, or ask a relevant follow-up question.

items.question: What can I do if I am unsure about workplace conversation habits?

children.text: Observe how coworkers socialize during breaks and ask about expectations if needed.

sections.question: Which action best helps build a professional relationship after someone gives you advice?
sections.explanation: A thank-you note shows appreciation and supports an ongoing professional relationship.

children.text: An informational interview is a chance to learn about a person’s organization and career journey. Preparing questions, listening carefully, and following up can help turn an introduction into a professional relationship.
Hypothetical example:

Priya asks a professional in her field for an informational interview. She prepares questions about the person’s career journey, listens carefully, and later sends a brief thank-you note with a related follow-up question.

items.question: What can I ask during an informational interview?

children.text: Ask about the organization, workplace culture, and the person’s career journey.

items.question: How can I prepare for a job fair?

children.text: Research the participating companies you plan to approach so you can show informed interest.

sources.title: Seven Easy Steps to Find a Mentor

sections.question: Which factor directly affects fuel expenses?
sections.explanation: Fuel expenses are directly related to buying location, vehicle fuel consumption, and time of year.

children.text: A useful car budget considers several cost categories. Maintenance can include preventative work, repairs, tires, and miscellaneous expenses.
Hypothetical example:
A driver comparing a car with public transit lists expected fuel, parking, preventative maintenance, repairs, and tire costs before deciding which option fits their needs.

items.question: Why can fuel costs differ by location?

children.text: Gasoline prices vary across provinces and territories, including because fuel taxes differ.

items.question: What does vehicle maintenance include?

children.text: It includes preventative maintenance, repairs outside the manufacturer warranty, tires, and miscellaneous expenses.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.6: Resources if You’re in Financial Difficulty

sections.question: Which is a warning sign when someone offers debt help?

options.text: They guarantee they can erase your debt

sections.explanation: A guarantee to erase debt is a warning sign. Be cautious of quick-fix promises, large upfront payments, and high-pressure sales tactics.

children.text: Check a debt professional’s credentials and be cautious of guaranteed fixes. Licensed Insolvency Trustees are federally regulated and must explain available options, including alternatives to insolvency.
Hypothetical example:

Priya sees an advertisement promising to erase her debt. She does not pay the requested upfront fee. Instead, she checks the professional’s credentials and looks for reliable information about her options.

items.question: What warning signs should I notice in a debt-help offer?

children.text: Watch for guaranteed debt or credit-score fixes, large upfront payments, high-pressure sales tactics, or advice to take a high-interest loan to pay fees.

items.question: Who can provide government-regulated insolvency options?

children.text: Licensed Insolvency Trustees are the only federally regulated professionals authorized to provide consumer proposals or bankruptcies in Canada.

sources.title: Let’s Talk Money and Break the Stigma around debt
sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

sections.question: When should you provide a reference list to an employer?

options.text: When the employer specifically requests it
Before asking the references for permission

sections.explanation: Job Bank recommends keeping references on a separate sheet and providing them only when specifically requested.

children.text: A reference list should be separate from your resume and ready to share if an employer asks for it.
Hypothetical example:
An employer asks Sam for references after an interview. Sam confirms that the references are prepared, then sends the separate reference sheet.

items.question: Should references appear on my resume?

children.text: No. Keep them on a separate sheet and provide them when specifically requested.

items.question: What should I do before sending my reference list?

children.text: Confirm that each person has agreed to be a reference and knows they may be contacted.

sources.title: How to write a good resume

sections.question: Which action can limit what non-followers see on a personal social media profile?
sections.explanation: Making a profile private can limit what non-followers see.

children.text: Privacy settings can limit what non-followers see. Positive interactions with organizations can also support networking and help you find opportunities.
Hypothetical example:
Sam makes a personal profile private, then uses a professional account to follow an organization and leave a positive, thoughtful comment on its post.

items.question: What kind of profile photo does WorkBC suggest?

children.text: A clear, recent photo that accurately represents you, such as a headshot.

items.question: How can social media support networking?

children.text: You can follow organizations, make positive comments, and contact people in a field that interests you.

sections.question: On TransLink, what should you do before boarding when passengers are leaving?
sections.explanation: Waiting for passengers to exit first keeps the doorway clear and makes boarding safer and easier.

children.text: Courtesy supports accessibility. Priority seats near the doors are intended for people with mobility needs, including needs that may not be visible.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is sitting in a priority seat when another passenger asks to use it. Sam takes the request at face value, gives up the seat, and moves away from the doors.

items.question: How should I carry a backpack on busy TransLink transit?

children.text: Remove it to make more room for other passengers.

items.question: Where should personal belongings be kept on a TransLink bus?

children.text: Keep them out of aisles, doorways, exits, and seats so they do not create a tripping hazard.

sections.question: Which change should you report to IRCC for an application in progress?
sections.explanation: IRCC lists a new passport as a change to report. Include proof of the change.

children.text: Life changes can affect information in an application. IRCC needs current information to review and decide on an application. The method for reporting a change may depend on the type of information and application.
Hypothetical example:
Sam gets married while an application is in progress. Sam reports the change through the appropriate IRCC process and includes proof of the marriage.

items.question: Should I include proof when reporting a life change?

children.text: Yes. IRCC says to include proof of the change.

items.question: Should I keep checking my old contact information after an update?

children.text: Yes. IRCC may use the old information until the update is complete.

sources.title: Update your application (submit new information we didn’t request)

sections.question: Which service lets you book and drive a shared car yourself without buying or leasing one?
sections.explanation: A car-sharing program lets members book and drive a shared car. A rideshare trip provides a driver, so the passenger does not drive the car.

children.text: Match the transportation option to the trip. A rental may suit a longer trip, while car-sharing may suit occasional short-term use.
Hypothetical example:
Sam usually takes transit but needs a car for an occasional errand. Sam researches local car-sharing programs to see whether one meets that need.

items.question: Are car-sharing programs available everywhere?

children.text: No. They are available in some cities, so check what operates locally.

items.question: What should I check in a car rental agreement?

children.text: Check whether car insurance is included if you need it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Keeping Your PR: Time in Canada and Time Abroad

sections.question: Which time abroad may count toward a permanent resident's residency obligation?

options.text: A vacation taken alone, with no qualifying work or family-accompaniment condition
Full-time work for the Canadian federal, provincial, or territorial government
A trip with a friend, with no qualifying work or family-accompaniment condition

sections.explanation: Time abroad may count under qualifying full-time work or family-accompaniment rules. A vacation taken alone does not count when no qualifying exception applies. For example, accompanying a Canadian-citizen spouse or common-law partner may qualify.

children.text: The reason for time abroad matters. IRCC considers what the permanent resident does abroad and whether they accompany an eligible spouse, partner, or parent.
Hypothetical example:
Sam works full-time outside Canada for a provincial government. Sam records the travel dates and keeps an employer letter so the circumstances can be documented.

items.question: Does an expired PR card automatically end PR status?

children.text: No. A person remains a permanent resident until an official decision or another listed event changes that status.

items.question: Can an expired PR card be used as a travel document?

children.text: No. IRCC says an expired PR card cannot be used as a travel document.

sources.title: Online Help Centre - List of questions and answers

sections.question: Which document confirms that a school has admitted you?
sections.explanation: A letter of acceptance confirms admission. Financial records show available funds, while a passport is a travel and identity document.

children.text: For a program longer than 6 months, the acceptance letter must come from a designated learning institution. Financial proof must cover tuition, living expenses, and return transportation, including costs for accompanying family members.
Hypothetical example:

Sam receives an acceptance letter for a program longer than 6 months. Before applying, Sam checks that the school is a designated learning institution and organizes financial records showing the required types of expenses.

items.question: Is a study permit the same as a visa?

children.text: No. A study permit is not a visa. If the application is approved, the government also provides a visitor visa or electronic travel authorization when required.

items.question: Does studying in Quebec involve an additional document?

children.text: Most international students in programs longer than six months need a Québec Acceptance Certificate (CAQ), unless an exemption applies. Check Québec’s authorization and exemption rules for your situation before applying.

sources.title: Find out if you need a study permit
Required authorizations to study in Québec as a foreign national
